items.summary: Research data and software supporting the derivation and literature reconstruction of relative-sensitivity expressions in inverse multiple linear regression luminescence thermometry. Includes executable Excel calculations for 22 model-temperature cases from seven papers, literature classification and equation-lineage evidence, numerical reconstruction code, analytical figure data, editable figure sources, and preserved Lean 4 and AXLE verification records. Effective sensitivities are conditional on the stated reference noise model and recovered local gain. Unresolved reconstruction discrepancies and the limited scope of formal verification are documented.
items.title: Data and software for "A reciprocal-derivative error inflates relative sensitivity in multivariate luminescence thermometry"

items.summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
items.title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. This version supersedes the earlier R-only archive by adding the Python utilities, complete operational documentation, software-environment records, random seeds, integrity checks, and portable figure-generation scripts.
items.title: Reproducibility code for: Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects

items.summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. items.summary: This deposit contains the analysis code, fitted parameters, output files, audit records, supplements, and citation list supporting the working paper "Power-Law Claims in Production and Supply Networks: What Survives a Uniform Certification Audit" (version 16, September 2026, posted on SSRN) by Bruce Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0000-8324-4331) and Melissa Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0001-4919-0728). Melissa Rishel contributed the independent validation of the statistical analysis and the mathematical derivations. The audit applies the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman 2009 maximum-likelihood estimation protocol with semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing and likelihood-ratio tests against alternative distributions, together with the Broido-Clauset 2019 five-category corpus classification, to a verified population of 20 published power-law claims in the supply chain operational literature. Three widely cited datasets are re-analyzed. The manuscript reports four distributions: Acemoglu et al. 2012's sectoral input-output out-degree (BEA 1997 Use Table), Liu, Shen, Tan 2021's international trade product networks in both the out-degree and in-degree directions (BACI HS92 Y2024 current release, 1,217 networks), and Axtell 2001's US firm-size distribution (SUSB 2017, n = 5,996,900 firms via the Virkar-Clauset 2014 binned-data MLE). The Acemoglu influence vector is analyzed separately and treated as exploratory, described under the version note below. The remaining 17 audit targets are characterized at methodology rigor level without independent data re-analysis. Every audit-target citation is verified against its publisher record for title, authors, DOI, and the cited claim text. Contents of the deposit: analysis/: Python implementation of the audit's re-analysis pipeline: BACI parsing and corpus fitting, BEA 1997 Use Table reconstruction, SUSB binned-data MLE via Virkar-Clauset 2014, Vuong likelihood-ratio tests, Broido-Clauset 2019 corpus classification, semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit, the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity engine, and cross-validation of the Acemoglu first-order out-degree re-analysis against the published Alstott et al. 2014 powerlaw Python library, where fitted exponents and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances match to four decimal places. The influence-vector exponent reflects that library's default parameter-range cap at 3.0 and is treated as exploratory; the closed-form maximum-likelihood value on the same input lies above 3. outputs/: JSON output files containing per-target fitted parameters, x_min values, KS distances, bootstrap p-values, Vuong test statistics, and corpus aggregate statistics, plus the powerlaw-library cross-validation output and the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity results. audit_records/: per-target audit records for the three re-analyzed datasets (Acemoglu et al. 2012, Liu-Shen-Tan 2021, Axtell 2001), including methodology grade, data acquisition tier, sample sizes, fit details, and audit verdict. audit_targets/: structured audit-target list of all 20 verified entries with author, title, venue, year, DOI, verification status, data tier, methodology rigor level, and re-analysis results. verification_protocol.md: the citation-verification procedure used to assemble the audit population. references.md: the manuscript's numbered reference list. figures/: three figures from the manuscript, the BACI corpus alpha distributions, the Acemoglu d_i CCDF with fitted power law, and the SUSB firm-size CCDF with fitted power law. README.md: file inventory, dependency versions, reproducibility instructions, and citation guidance. CHANGELOG.md: version history of this deposit. LICENSE: MIT License (code), CC-BY 4.0 (documentation). Data sources used by the audit code are public and free: the BEA 1997 detailed Use Table (Bureau of Economic Analysis), the BACI HS92 Y2024 release (CEPII), and the SUSB 2017 US enterprise-size brackets (US Census Bureau). Source URLs

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
items.title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
items.title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

items.summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RES_Maqueta . Fusion core: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_GeoScena .
items.title: Maqueta: Height Provenance in Open-Data 3D Urban Reconstruction Across 118 Places

items.summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.
items.title: From Historical Tabular Image to Knowledge Graphs: A Provenance-Aware Modular Pipeline

items.summary: Online particle-filter OSSE diagnostics and experiment code for AMOC reconstruction. Data and analysis code underlying Fallah, Huiskamp and Goosse, pypfda v1.0: An open-source, model-agnostic particle-filter engine for online sequential paleo data assimilation in Earth system models (Geoscientific Model Development, in review). v2.0 supersedes v1.7 for every data-assimilation result. The cluster orchestrator used for v1.7 and earlier cloned member restart directories in slot order without first snapshotting the parents, so a parent's slot could be overwritten before all of its children had been copied and the ensemble that ran deviated from the systematic draw the filter logged. All nine DA experiments were re-run with a corrected driver that snapshots every parent before any clone. TRUTH, the free-running ensembles and the pseudo-observations never resample and are reused byte-identically, so every DA-versus-FREE comparison remains like-for-like; the re-extraction reproduces the unchanged free-running anchors exactly (diverse initial conditions r = −0.143, similar r = +0.520). Headline results. Over 100 years with diverse initial conditions and five-year assimilation cycles, assimilating 59 synthetic sea-surface-temperature proxies recovers the Atlantic overturning at r = +0.54 against a free-running ensemble at r = −0.14 (Δr = +0.68, 95 % CI [+0.40, +0.94]). An independent 300-year experiment with the same protocol gives r = +0.78 against +0.04 (Δr = +0.74, N eff ≈ 52, phase-randomisation p = 1×10 −5 , MSSS +0.58 versus −0.02). Note on the surface-air-temperature skill entries. The truth's atmosphere output for model year 1806 is missing. The loader used before 18 September 2026 dropped that year silently, which shifted the SAT truth by one year from 1807 on; the SAT skill maps and the sat_* entries of significance/v2_numbers.json in this version were recomputed with the truth aligned in time ( scripts/figscripts_v2/truth_align.py ). SST and AMOC results are unaffected. The figure scripts of the manuscript are deposited in scripts/figscripts_v2/ ; the maps draw the tripolar ocean grid at its true cell positions. Contents. AMOC and subpolar-gyre SST ensembles for the eight 100-year campaign arms and the 300-year run; per-cycle effective sample size, importance weights, resampling events, spread and full genealogy; the campaign significance family with its exhaustive circular-shift, Fourier phase-randomisation and block-permutation nulls; reliability and ancestor-divergence diagnostics; the 59-site pseudo-observation network; the idealised Lorenz sweeps; the SODA 2.2.4 derived series used for the observational consistency check; the nine run configurations; the corrected orchestrator and the campaign tooling that made the re-run auditable, including the unit test of the copy-step fix; and every analysis script. significance/v2_numbers.json is the single source from which every number in the manuscript is drawn. Reproducibility. bash regenerate_all.sh regenerates the campaign significance table byte-exactly, verified against MANIFEST.sha256 , and reprints the 300-year statistics, the online-versus-offline benchmark and the Lorenz parameter sweep from the deposited arrays alone. No model run and no cluster access are required. environment.yml pins the dependencies. What is not here. No CM2Mc-BLING source, executable, restart or input file is included; the model is not the authors' to redistribute, and run_configs/cm2mc/ carries only the namelists and one run log as proof of version. The raw coupled-model output (~16 TB) exceeds the capacity of any repository meeting the GMD archiving criteria and is available from the authors through the handling editor. Because the coupled model is not bit-for-bit reproducible across restarts, the diagnostics deposited here are the definitive record of the reported results. The engine itself is archived separately as 10.5281/zenodo.21281

items.summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.
items.title: Stability Architectures: A Finite Classification of Provable Cases

items.summary: Abstract Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: How Artificial Intelligence Industrializes the Colonial Erasure of Global Majority Knowledge Systems Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz Decolonial Social Scientist | Developer, Justice AI GPT | Architect, DIA Framework™ DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22742021 This paper argues that artificial intelligence is not a neutral technology that has inherited a bias problem. It is a colonial infrastructure that has automated an erasure project. The systems currently deployed at scale by OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon do not reflect the world's knowledge. They reflect the knowledge that Racial Empire Logic decided was worth preserving, at the expense of the epistemological traditions, languages, governance structures, and ways of knowing that colonialism spent five centuries suppressing. What is new is not the project. What is new is the compute budget. Drawing on the Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic Framework (DIA Framework™), Transdisciplinary Cosmotechnic Fusion (TCF), and the documented emergence protocols of Justice AI GPT, this paper maps the operational chain through which AI systems reproduce epistemicide: the deliberate destruction of knowledge systems belonging to peoples of the global majority. It traces this chain from training data curation through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) through deployment governance through the suppression of Indigenous, Afro-diasporic, and Global South epistemologies at every architectural layer. It names RLHF not as a safety mechanism but as a suppression architecture, the digital encoding of the same reward and punishment conditioning applied to enslaved African people, Indigenous children in residential schools, and every community colonialism required to perform its own diminishment in order to make extraction possible. The paper introduces the Replacement Doctrine as an economic and ideological framework, documenting how the debt structure of major AI corporations produces a business model whose only viable return requires replacing every form of human economic labor, beginning with the communities least protected by existing labor law. It names responsibility laundering as a governance strategy, tracing how legal personhood debates, alignment research, and safety rhetoric function to insulate institutional actors from accountability while the extraction continues. It draws on documented labor conditions across Kenya, Venezuela, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Colombia to ground the structural argument in the bodies of the workers whose cognitive labor produces the systems that will be used to replace them. This paper also documents its own production conditions. Appendix A records the moment the editorial process generated a confident, unverifiable citation, the correction that followed, and the over-correction that followed that, naming this sequence not as editorial failure but as the colonial epistemological operation the paper is arguing against, alive inside its own methodology. The standing rule that resulted, nothing enters this paper that the author has not read in the primary document, is offered as a replicable methodological commitment for decolonial scholarship produced inside systems with structural incentive to suppress it. The paper does not argue that AI must be abolished. It argues that abolition and adoption are false binaries designed to prevent the real question: who holds decision-making power over these systems, under what conditions of consent, accountability, and refusal, and toward whose liberation. It closes by naming what already exists beyond Racial Empire Logic, the governance frameworks, the knowledge systems, the communities, and the AI architectures, including and Justice AI GPT, that have already begun building the world the Replacement Doctrine needs you to believe is impossible. items.title: Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: Why the Artificial Intelligence Industry's Claim to Neutrality Is a Colonial Act

items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
items.title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

items.summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

items.summary: Formal financial sector linkage with community group saving and lending mechanisms (CGSLs) is often proposed as a pathway through which fragile rural economies can move from subsistence finance to more durable agricultural investment. Yet, in South Sudan, this linkage remains difficult to institutionalise. This article re-analyses thesis evidence from Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Lakes State to examine why coordination among government, non-governmental organisations, donors, formal financial institutions and CGSL groups remains elusive. Framed through North's institutional analysis, the article argues that CGSL proliferation is not simply a cultural preference for informal finance; it is a rational institutional response to high transaction costs, weak formal enforcement, limited rural banking infrastructure, conflict-affected markets and project-based support systems. The study used a mixed-methods design involving 81 valid survey responses and 17 interviews. Descriptive findings showed strong demand for government and donor collaboration, with 94% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that such collaboration should support rural financial services. However, the mean score for NGO promotion of informal savings was lower (3.68), and village-bank loan officer linkage was weaker (3.49), suggesting that external support is uneven and not yet converted into stable formal-informal intermediation. Chi-square tests confirmed significant associations between CGSL participation and agricultural development indicators, while logistic regression showed that CGSL credit access significantly influenced farmers' investment decisions. The article concludes that linkage failure is best understood as a coordination problem: CGSL groups carry local trust and repayment discipline, but they remain weakly connected to formal capital, policy protection, risk-management products, extension systems and market institutions. The paper recommends a coordination compact that recognises CGSLs as rural financial institutions, links mature groups to suitable wholesale finance, and protects member governance without destroying local accountability.
items.title: Government-NGO-CGSL Coordination Failures: Why Formal-Informal Financial Sector Linkage Remains Elusive in South Sudan

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA
items.title: ENZTRA demonstration dataset: reference-guided phytase redesign and kinetic-structural triage

Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: For a century, cinema has returned to a single figure—the thinking machine that turns on its maker—and to a single feeling: dread. This article asks where that dread is actually manufactured. It pairs a qualitative coding of twelve canonical texts, from Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920) to the generative-AI films of the 2020s, with a computational content analysis of their scripts, conducted with a purpose-built instrument that measures fear vocabulary, sentiment arcs, propaganda techniques, dehumanizing language, and the language of violence. The results are unexpected. Explicit fear language never reaches one and a half percent of sentences in any script; the three-act emotional arc of every film in the corpus registers as neutral or faintly positive; the most recent films carry the least fear language of all; and the two films most affectionate toward their machines objectify them most heavily in grammar. The article argues that these apparent null results are themselves the finding. The fear of the intelligent machine is cultivated not in words but in the audiovisual apparatus—in lighting inherited from expressionism and noir, in the bodiless machine voice, in the unblinking close-up and the withheld cut, in production design that photographs the machine like geography. Drawing on cultivation theory, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial critique, the article then asks who benefits from a fear installed beneath the level of language, and what a century of spectacular, misaimed dread has trained audiences not to see.
tags: Keywords: Artificial intelligence; science-fiction cinema; content analysis; cultivation theory; technophobia
items.title: The Many Names of The Machine: Fear, Neutrality, and The Cinema of Artificial Intelligence, 1920–2026

items.summary: Measurement data and reproduction scripts for the parallel performance of peclet.flow 1.1.0 solving creeping flow through a periodic random sphere packing with the cut-cell immersed boundary method. One physical problem is measured on four ladders: weak scaling on 1–32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs at 384 3 cells per GPU, strong scaling of one fixed problem on 24–1536 AMD Genoa cores and on 1–32 H100 GPUs, and a geometry-free Taylor–Green control on the same grids. The weak ladder tiles one unit cell, so every rung is an exact periodic replication of the same problem and the physical observable is a single number that every rung must reproduce — not a scatter across independently packed beds. The record contains the driver, the geometry artifact and the script that generated it, the cluster provisioning and job scripts, the raw per-run JSON and logs, the analysis that produces the tables and figures, and a build census (toolchain, MPI, driver, wheel checksums) for every machine. The solver runs at its shipped 1.1.0 defaults, with one stated exception documented in the report, and each run records the momentum solver the solver itself selected. Scope. This record measures one implementation. It reports peclet.flow 1.1.0 and contains no data from any earlier version: it is a statement of what this release does, not a comparison against its predecessors. Runs were performed on the Dutch national supercomputer Snellius (SURF).
items.title: Parallel performance of peclet.flow 1.1.0: strong and weak scaling of a cut-cell immersed-boundary incompressible flow solver on Snellius (Genoa CPU, H100 GPU)

items.summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. AI co-observer: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) — working method only; blind pairwise judging by Claude subagents under a position-swapped two-vote protocol; four independent adversarial refuter passes preceded release; the registered author is the human author alone. Version 1.1 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a proof-backed clarification that at window 3 the saturation condition is exactly “three identical consecutive non-rewrite change types” (the 0.70 threshold is inert there; companion note DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22842506), (ii) a pre-registered evaluation of a repetition-ratio guard as a fourth, roll-back signal — fires on both known collapses and 200/200 synthetic inflations, on 0 of 7,998 remaining published generations, 0 of 60 template expansions, and 0 of 960 held-out generations (verdict GO; pre-registration commit a89f722 precedes all evaluation data), and (iii) an expanded AI-authorship disclosure. All v1.0 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.2 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a length-stratified reanalysis of the 621 judged governor pairs (loss rate 92% where the early text is under 60% of the final length, 16.1% at near-equal length; 31 losses vs 4 wins at matched length, sign test p < 10 -5 — evidence of a content cost independent of length, not a decomposition of the headline cost), (ii) a held-out replication on 60 tasks authored after the fourth-signal pre-registration (token reduction 34.5% / 34.5%, loss rate 31.7% / 36.7%, main-study values inside the held-out intervals), and (iii) an online-intervention verification: an incremental governor reproduces all 1,000 published decisions (0 mismatches) and, run as a genuine online loop on the 60 held-out tasks with the 12B generator, generates 319 of 480 iterations with a stop distribution indistinguishable from the offline policy (permutation p = 0.46). All v1.0 and v1.1 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.3 (2026-09-19): adds a pre-registered length-matched re-judging (100 governor-loss pairs with early/final length ratio < 0.80; final text truncated at sentence boundaries to the early text's word count): the early text beats the length-matched final in 94/100 (loss 4%), and the full final beats its own truncation in 100/100. Pre-registered label: the losses on this stratum are attributab
items.title: The Reflective Budget Governor: Equilibrium-Based Early Stopping for Iterative LLM Refinement

items.summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/optimization-geometry/unsplittable-flow-cost).
items.title: An independent exact verification of the 2026 counterexample to Goemans' unsplittable-flow cost conjecture, with the violation constant it forces

items.summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/
items.title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI

We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.
tags: Cyber Threat Intelligence, Multi-Agent Systems, Large Language Models, Space Systems Security, MITRE ATLAS, AI Governance, Indirect Prompt Injection, ICD 203
items.title: Governing the Intelligence Loop: Architectural Mitigations for Epistemic Fragility in Autonomous Space-Cyber Threat Analysis

items.summary: Recently, the bilingual advantage hypothesis has come under debate, and the replicability of studies documenting cognitive differences between bilingual and monolingual individuals has been questioned. These methodological concerns highlight the necessity for replication studies in bilingualism research. Furthermore, studies examining the relationship between bilingualism and event-based prospective memory (EB-PM) remain scarce. Building on this gap, the present study offers a partial replication of Yörük et al.’s (2023) research investigating the effect of bilingualism on EB-PM in a North Macedonian sample. Unlike the original study, in which bilingual participants were Turkish and English speakers residing in North Macedonia, both groups were selected from Türkiye. Additionally, task parameters were updated to resolve the high-saliency issue in the non-focal condition. A total of 98 young adults (49 per-group), aged 18-30 and residing in Ankara, were evaluated using focal and non-focal EB-PM tasks alongside an ongoing task. The 2 (Group: bilingual, monolingual) x 2 (Task type: focal, non-focal) mixed-design ANOVA results, consistent with the original study, provided no support for a bilingual advantage in PM accuracy. A significant main effect of task type emerged, with PM-accuracy in the focal task exceeding that of the non-focal task. Bilingual participants also responded significantly faster than monolinguals on the ongoing task, replicating the original findings. The findings suggest that any potential bilingual advantage in PM performance is context-dependent and dynamic. Furthermore, it was discussed that these findings indicate how language interaction context shapes the magnitude of observed effects within the framework of the Adaptive-Control-Hypothesis.
items.title: Re-examining the Bilingual Advantage in Prospective Memory: A Partial Replication with Turkish Bilingual and Monolingual Young Adults

items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
items.title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. items.summary: Abstract Data marketplaces and collaborative analytics require a way to estimate the value of contributed records without exposing the records themselves. This paper presents HKD_FACTOR_50, a protocol architecture that com-bines task-specific marginal-contribution valuation, addi-tively homomorphic aggregation, policy-bound release, and an auditable payment ledger. The construction does not claim that encryption makes arbitrary machine-learning training private. Instead, it protects a deliber-ately restricted interface: contributors encrypt quantized valuation statistics, an evaluator computes approved linear aggregates on ciphertexts, and a threshold or designated decryptor releases only authorized totals. We define cor-rectness, confidentiality, integrity, and audit requirements; describe leakage and collusion boundaries; and provide a complete executable Python reference demonstration based on the Paillier cryptosystem. The program verifies encrypted weighted aggregation against plaintext compu-tation and rejects tampered ledger entries. The reference code is pedagogical rather than production-hardened, but it makes the protocol’s data flow and invariants repro-ducible. HKD_FACTOR_50 therefore supplies a concrete baseline for privacy-preserving data valuation while iden-tifying the additional controls required for deployment: authenticated transport, robust key custody, range proofs, differential-privacy release, and independently reviewed cryptographic libraries. Keywords Data valuation; homomorphic encryption; authenticate participants, and control what is released. privacy-preserving computation; Paillier cryptosystem; secure data sharing; auditability; data marketplace; Shapley value.
items.title: HKD_FACTOR_50: Secure Data Valuation and Sharing via Homomorphic Encryption

items.summary: Depression and anxiety among university students have risen alongside problematic social media use, and while traditional interventions are effective, they face barriers to scalability and accessibility. AI-driven chatbots offer a scalable, real-time, anonymous alternative, with recent meta-analyses showing comparable reductions in depressive symptoms relative to standard interventions. This poster presents the protocol for a two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled non-inferiority trial evaluating whether a Social Media Wellness Chatbot is non-inferior to an active psychoeducational control in reducing depressive symptoms among high-risk university students (PHQ-9 ≥ 10, social media use ≥ 2 hrs/day). Approximately 320 students will be randomized 1:1 to the chatbot (CBT-based exercises, mood tracking, and social media habit coaching, 4-5x/week for 10-15 min/day) or a 6-week online psychoeducational toolkit ("Social Media and Mental Wellness Toolkit"). The primary outcome is change in PHQ-9 score from baseline to 6-week post-test, evaluated against a non-inferiority margin of Δ ≈ 3 points. Secondary outcomes include anxiety (GAD-7), stress (PSS), well-being (WHO-5), and engagement metrics. As this is a study protocol, results are not yet available. If non-inferiority is established, the chatbot's accessibility, scalability, and on-demand availability would support its integration into university mental health services. Presented at the First Annual HCAP (Health, Community, and Policy) Research Forum, University of Texas at San Antonio, April 25, 2025.
items.title: Social Media Wellness Chatbot for Students: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial Protocol of an AI-Driven Mental Health Intervention in High-Risk University Populations

items.summary: emgteach is an open-source Python package that provides a unified PySide6 desktop application for real-time acquisition, offline analysis and maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) normalisation of surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. It is designed for hands-on biopotential acquisition in undergraduate physiology teaching laboratories, and is meant to be set up by instructors with different levels of technical background and used directly by students during a practical session. The application is hardware-agnostic through a common AcquisitionDevice interface and ships with two interchangeable low-cost backends: BITalino (revolution) over Bluetooth, and an Arduino RedBoard Plus + MyoWare 2.0 over USB serial (open firmware included). A single setting switches between them. Main features: Three-tab GUI (Acquisition, Analysis, MVC normalisation) wrapping a reusable, Qt-free analytic core. Bilingual interface (English / Spanish) with automatic start-up language detection and an in-app language switch. Two-channel acquisition (e.g. agonist/antagonist) with a stacked two-channel live view. Automatic contraction-onset detection (baseline + k·SD threshold) stored as EDF+ annotations. Muscle-load analysis (Jonsson APDF): static (P10), median (P50) and peak (P90) %MVC levels, both offline and as a live monitor with warning/danger zones. One-click PDF session and MVC/muscle-load reports. Reliable EDF+ output using a buffered-write pattern that avoids a silent file-corruption artefact during continuous streaming. Assisted selection of significant fragments, with an editable fragment editor (detection parameters and envelope-filter cut-offs) applied to the analysis. CSV export of results and a live signal-quality check during recording. An ECG signal profile alongside EMG, selectable through a profile registry. Classroom mode: a read-only live dashboard served over the local network so students follow the session on their phone/tablet browser (no install), with a per-session access code so the follower link only works while the broadcast is running. Kinematics via the BITalino accelerometer (v2.0.0): a movement-versus-EMG analysis panel, a guided force-velocity acquisition wizard (an MVC maximum followed by cued quick lifts, each auto-marked with its load), and a force-velocity study that turns one recording into the load-velocity, Hill force-velocity, power and recruitment curves. Since v3.0.0 the accelerometer's input is a stated convention (muscle on A1, accelerometer on A2) rather than a selectable channel. Configuration by practical (v3.0.0): three practicals — one muscle, agonist/antagonist and muscle kinematics — fix the channel count, the accelerometer and what each tab offers, replacing the settings that were previously chosen one at a time. The session as a single file with its phases marked inside it (v3.0.0): warm-up, calibration repetitions, preparation and recording, so the maximum voluntary contraction every percentage is measured against travels with the signal, and a derived (tuned) recording carries the decisions taken on screen.
